strategy.headline: Six banners sell themselves; Nike wins Chicago by dressing the Hawk-season walk to Madison in the city's own codes
strategy.thesis: Chicago buys the Bulls as a six-banner religion, so 1990s red-and-black moves through a 31-51 season and a ground-up rebuild without Nike lifting a finger. The upside is in what the market does not yet have: a city that sorts itself by side, high school and grid number, plays half the year in Park District fieldhouses, and invented house, the community mural, JB skating and the original March Madness. It shops in cold-weather bursts from the pre-freeze November drop through Dec 20, with tourists on the Mag Mile and taste set in West Loop, Wicker Park and South Side doors. Nike wins by letting Jordan Brand own the dynasty, making outerwear the hero and using Madison Street, the line where North and South addresses begin and the Bulls' own street, as the one-city story the Splitter-era core can grow into.

archetype.name: The Six-Banner Congregation
archetype.description: A multigenerational, all-sides faith in the 1991-98 Bulls that keeps buying through losing seasons but greets every rebuild promise with South Side and West Side sarcasm. It is loyal to the banners and the red-and-black, while the roster has to earn its place.

pulse.teamMoment: Year one of a new regime: Billy Donovan stepped down, Tiago Splitter took over as coach and EVP Bryson Graham is building a size-first 'SLAP' roster around Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson, with Norman Powell and Nic Claxton added. The Bulls are coming off 31-51, are rated low in power rankings and have no opening-night or Christmas Day game, so the Emirates NBA Cup's East Group C is their early stage.
pulse.sentiment: Guarded hope wrapped in ownership fatigue: fans like the draft and Wilson's All-Summer League debut but have learned to mock hype and wait for proof.

topInsights.title: Heritage is the floor, not the growth
topInsights.insight: Jordan 23, Pippen 33 and Rodman 91 still rival current jerseys at the United Center, and every retail lens says heritage outsells the roster regardless of record. The art lens warns that another '90s throwback cycle in a rebuild year reads as filler, so the dynasty is the baseline, not the news.
topInsights.implication: Keep heritage as an evergreen, Jordan Brand-coordinated layer and put new design energy into civic, neighborhood and new-core stories. Don't overbuy current-player inventory before Wilson proves himself.

topInsights.title: The Hawk writes the merchandise plan
topInsights.insight: The home season runs through the months when lake wind makes 20 degrees feel like zero. Fans walk from the Ashland Green/Pink stop in a parka with a hoodie under the jersey, outdoor runs move into fieldhouses from November to April, and spend peaks between the first freeze and Dec 20.
topInsights.implication: Make the wind-blocking stadium parka, heavyweight fleece and cuffed knit the hero Bulls products, landing before the first freeze. Tees and shorts are a compressed June-to-August business.

topInsights.title: Madison Street makes the Bulls the one team every side shares
topInsights.insight: Addresses count from State and Madison, and the United Center sits at 1901 W. Madison, on the line between North and South addresses, while the Cubs and Sox split the city by side. Chicagoans place each other by side, grid number and 'Where'd you go to high school?', and the Public League even names conferences Red-South and Red-West.
topInsights.implication: Build North/South/West/suburb product that adds up to one city: grid coordinates, area codes (312, 773, 708, 630, 847) and school-and-side tags, sold where each side shops.

topInsights.title: The swap-proof culture is Black-built and born near the arena
topInsights.insight: House was named at The Warehouse on Jefferson, less than two miles east of the United Center. The South Side gave the country the Wall of Respect, AfriCOBRA's 'Kool-Aid colors', JB skating at The Rink on 87th, footwork and Simeon's Public League dynasty. No other NBA market can claim any of it.
topInsights.implication: These are the strongest stories Nike can design from, and they only work co-authored and paid: Chosen Few DJs, AfriCOBRA members and estates, JB crews and South Side institutions, credited by name, with no generic 'Chicago party' or Pan-African shorthand.

topInsights.title: Jordan owns the shoe, rivals own the hometown heroes
topInsights.insight: Sneakerheads worldwide call the white, red and black AJ1 'Chicagos', but the city's favorite sons largely sit with rival brands: Derrick Rose and Candace Parker with adidas, Angel Reese with Reebok, Joe Freshgoods with New Balance. Nike's own local assets are Mac Irvin Fire, the Bulls and Sky uniforms, Notre and Jordan Brand's Don C lineage.
topInsights.implication: Don't ship another white-red-black colorway or borrow Rose's No. 1 or his Englewood story. Win with new materials and stories, grassroots investment through Mac Irvin Fire and Park District gyms, and boutique partners with Nike history.

topInsights.title: Lights-out is the Bulls' in-building signature
topInsights.insight: The darkened arena, the roving spotlights and the starting-lineup intro carried from Chicago Stadium into the rebuild are the team's most recognized gameday moment, and fans treat 'Sirius' as shorthand for the whole ritual.
topInsights.implication: Blackout bases with reflective or glow Bulls-red beams make pregame and warm-up product feel made in the building, without licensing the song: never name it or use it on product.

topInsights.title: A rebuild needs stories that don't need a superstar
topInsights.insight: Fans who have learned to be skeptical will mock rebuild slogans, but Chicago has Big Shoulders and 'I Will' civic language for a size-and-physicality roster. It also has the Chicago-made NBA Jam, whose Bulls famously had no Jordan, and a Chicago-born Lithuanian-American forward in Buzelis.
topInsights.implication: Use workwear 'build' textures, public-domain civic type and ensemble graphics (duo select-screens, a roster-as-mixtape tracklist) for Giddey, Buzelis and Wilson rather than hype copy. Stage rookie product after the first month.

collection.name: Big Shoulders
collection.story: Chicago calls itself the City of the Big Shoulders and 'The City That Works', and the new Bulls are being built on size and physicality. The collection keeps the 1966 bull and the red-and-black as fixed points and builds outward from the city's own working materials: the wind, the grid, the fieldhouse and the blackout before tip-off.

uniform.narrative: Every Chicago address counts out from State and Madison, and the Bulls play on Madison, the line where North and South begin, which makes them the team every side shares in a city that splits its baseball. The uniform draws its code from the grid, the street sign and Sullivan's cast iron at the zero point, not from the flag-and-skyline cues earlier City Editions leaned on. It gives the Splitter-era core a civic identity of its own without leaning on the Jordan years.
motifs: A hairline street-grid texture across the body, with the Madison line as a single red rule at the waist
Redrawn Sullivan ornament as a tonal black-on-black jacquard on the side panels
Hundred-block grid numbers ('1901 W') in the corner of the chest, like a Chicago street sign
A small brown honorary-street-sign tab saluting Chicago hoops, used once per season set
uniform.typography: A 'CHICAGO' wordmark in custom condensed street-sign capitals, drawn by a Chicago type designer, with Bulls block numerals outlined in red, and limestone and small grid coordinates under the number.
details: Neck tape: '1901 W MADISON' in limestone
Jock tag: '0 N/S · 0 E/W', the State and Madison zero point
Waistband: NORTH · WEST · SOUTH in grid type, so the sides read as one line
Inner collar: 'I WILL', the public-domain 1890s civic motto
Court tie-in: grid lines and hundred-block numbers inlaid in the sideline maple, with the Madison line running through center court
avoid: Full Chicago-flag prints, a fifth star or any repeat of the flag-and-skyline cues earlier City Editions used
The Jumpman, Jordan's name or likeness, or any implied Jordan co-sign without Jordan Brand
Six-point stars combined with crowns, pitchforks or other gang-nation symbols, plus 'Chiraq', drill references or violence imagery
CTA signage, City seal or Y-device and CPS marks used without clearance, and copies of the Chicago Theatre sign
Any Native imagery: Chicago is Council of Three Fires homeland and the Blackhawks share the building

risks.risk: Cannibalizing or colliding with Jordan Brand, which owns the dynasty, the 'Chicago' AJ1 and Jordan's name and likeness.
risks.mitigation: Route all dynasty and Jumpman references through Jordan Brand, and give Nike Basketball's Bulls product new materials and civic stories instead of another white-red-black story.

risks.risk: Rebuild hype backfires with a skeptical fan base that is tired of ownership and has a low-rated roster.
risks.mitigation: Use understated 'build' and civic language, avoid title-window or slogan messaging, and keep current-player inventory lean until results justify more.

risks.risk: Exploiting or endangering communities: drill, 'Chiraq' and gang-nation symbols, Black food caricature, and Latino neighborhoods under federal immigration enforcement since fall 2025.
risks.mitigation: Have community partners review every graphic. Work only through paid, credited local authors, and run bilingual, community-led activations in Pilsen, Little Village and Humboldt Park that collect no data and film no residents.

risks.risk: Rival-brand hometown heroes: Derrick Rose and Candace Parker (adidas), Angel Reese (Reebok) and Joe Freshgoods (New Balance).
risks.mitigation: Never use their names, numbers or stories. Compete through assets Nike owns (Mac Irvin Fire, the Bulls and Sky uniforms, Notre) and through grassroots investment.

risks.risk: Third-party IP: the city flag, seal and Y device, CTA marks, CPS and IHSA marks, 'March Madness', the 'Sirius' intro music, restaurant trade dress and 'Three-Peat'.
risks.mitigation: Clear licenses before concepting, redraw rather than copy, and keep songs, stand logos and trademarked phrases off product unless they are licensed.

scorecard.rationale: Chicago is one of the league's deepest design cultures and a global heritage retail engine with a full flagship, arena, boutique and suburban-mall network. Fan intensity scores high on legacy but is held back by a 31-51 rebuild and ownership fatigue, so the near-term upside is in civic and outerwear product more than in current-player demand.

music.headline: Chicago invented electric blues, gospel, house and footwork, and the Bulls still come out in the dark to 'Sirius': Nike's lane is the city's own Black-built sound, made with the DJs, poets and dancers who own it.
music.summary: Chicago's music history is a list of inventions: electric blues on South Michigan Avenue's Record Row, gospel at Bronzeville's Pilgrim Baptist, house at The Warehouse in the West Loop, then footwork, drill, and a poetry-slam rap lineage that runs from Common to Chance the Rapper, Noname and Saba. The team's own sound is older than its roster. It is the lights-out starting-lineup intro to the Alan Parsons Project's 'Sirius,' carried from the Jordan years into the Giddey-Buzelis-Wilson rebuild, and the 2020 All-Star Game at the United Center showed that an all-Chicago lineup (Chaka Khan, Common, Chance, Jennifer Hudson) can carry a night. House is the strongest story for product because no other city can claim it: it was born less than two miles east of the arena, and it lives on through a summer calendar of Blues Fest in June, the Chosen Few Picnic in July, Bud Billiken and Frankie Knuckles Day in August, and ARC on Labor Day weekend. The risks are just as local: drill is tied to real violence and an active federal case, and two of the city's biggest names, R. Kelly and Kanye West, are off-limits.

insights.title: House was born under two miles from the United Center
insights.detail: The Warehouse at 206 S. Jefferson St. gave house music its name through Frankie Knuckles' sets from 1977, Ron Hardy took it rawer at the Music Box, and WBMX's Hot Mix 5 radio mixes carried it into every South and West Side home. The block is now signed Frankie Knuckles Way, and the city marks Aug. 25 as Frankie Knuckles Day.
insights.implication: House is the Bulls' most swap-proof cultural export and it comes from the team's own side of town, so it should anchor a city collection co-made with house institutions like the Chosen Few DJs, not borrowed as a party aesthetic.

insights.title: The Bulls' anthem is a lights-out ritual
insights.detail: Since the mid-1980s the Bulls have introduced starters in a darkened arena to the Alan Parsons Project's 1982 instrumental 'Sirius,' with roving spotlights. Ray Clay's 1990s calls made it one of the most imitated intros in sports. The ritual links Jordan's Chicago Stadium, 'the Madhouse on Madison,' to the current rebuild.
insights.implication: The darkness, the spotlight beams and the red glow belong to the Bulls without needing a music license. That makes them strong cues for pregame and warmup product, reflective or glow-in-the-dark, as long as the song itself isn't named or used without clearance.

insights.title: Chicago rap comes out of slam poetry, not just drill
insights.detail: Slam poetry was invented at Uptown's Green Mill in 1986. In the early 2010s, YOUmedia, the teen studio at Harold Washington Library, along with Young Chicago Authors' Louder Than a Bomb slam, produced Chance the Rapper, Noname, Saba, Mick Jenkins and Jamila Woods. Common, son of ABA player Lonnie Lynn, set the conscious-rap template in the 1990s.
insights.implication: Wordplay is the scene's real craft, so give Bulls product type-led graphics and copy written by paid local poet-rappers. Nike should back that youth creative pipeline as a sponsor rather than mine street mythology.

insights.title: The South and West Sides built dances that are sneaker culture
insights.detail: Footwork, the 160-BPM dance and music that grew out of ghetto house and juke battles, was pushed worldwide by RP Boo and by DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn's Teklife crew. Chicago stepping, meanwhile, is the smooth partner dance of Black Chicago's adult lounges and steppers' sets. Both dances live or die on footwear.
insights.implication: Footwork dancers are natural wear-testers and content creators for a Bulls-colored low-top court shoe, and the dance's foot-placement patterns can become graphics. Partner with crews and pay them; don't just cast them.

insights.title: Drill made Chicago famous and is the riskiest sound to touch
insights.detail: Chief Keef's 2012 'I Don't Like' and 'Love Sosa,' recorded around Parkway Gardens ('O-Block') in Woodlawn, turned Chicago drill into a global style. The genre is tied to real killings such as King Von's in 2020, and Lil Durk was arrested on federal murder-for-hire charges in 2024.
insights.implication: Drill shapes how young Chicago dresses, but Nike should stay out of its imagery, slang and artists. Reach the same audience through DJs, producers, dancers and sneaker culture.

insights.title: Blues and gospel give the market a heritage palette
insights.detail: Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and Willie Dixon electrified the Delta blues at Chess Records, 2120 S. Michigan Ave., which is now Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation. Thomas A. Dorsey created gospel music at Pilgrim Baptist in Bronzeville, and Buddy Guy, who turned 90 in July 2026, still anchors the South Loop at Legends.
insights.implication: These traditions support a vintage capsule built on club neon and record-label type, released around the free Chicago Blues Festival in June, with proceeds shared with Blues Heaven rather than lifting Chess marks.

insights.title: A new roster with no music face yet
insights.detail: We know of no public Chicago music ties for anyone in the new core of Giddey, No. 4 pick Caleb Wilson, Norman Powell and Nic Claxton. Chicago-born Matas Buzelis is the one hometown thread. The team's last big music moment was the 2020 All-Star Game at the United Center, when Chance played the halftime show, Common spoke the intros and Chaka Khan sang the anthem.
insights.implication: Nike can build the team's connection to the scene from scratch: pair Buzelis and Wilson with local artists for content and launches, and treat the 2020 all-local lineup as the template for a home-opener music moment.

places.why: A house and techno basement club since 1982 where Chicago's DJ lineage still plays every week, and the right room for an after-hours launch.

places.name: Gramaphone Records
places.why: The dance-music shop where Chicago house DJs have dug for 12-inch records for decades.

places.name: Dusty Groove
places.neighborhood: Ukrainian Village / Wicker Park (N. Ashland Ave.)
places.why: A soul, jazz and funk crate-digger institution whose sleeve-art archive is a visual reference library for Chicago soul.

places.name: Green Mill Cocktail Lounge
places.why: A 1907 jazz room with a famous green neon sign; its Sunday-night Uptown Poetry Slam, started in 1986, invented slam poetry.

places.name: Buddy Guy's Legends
places.why: Buddy Guy's own club, which remains the city's flagship blues room and hosts his annual January residency.

places.name: Harold Washington Library Center (YOUmedia)
places.why: The teen studio and open mic where Chance, Noname and Saba came up, which makes it the origin point of Chicago's 2010s rap renaissance.

places.name: WHPK 88.5 FM
places.why: A long-running University of Chicago community station whose hip-hop, house and juke shows give South Side DJs a regular platform.

people.name: Chosen Few DJs
people.role: House DJ collective founded by Wayne Williams
people.why: Its Jackson Park picnic, often called the 'Woodstock of house,' is Black Chicago's house family reunion, so the collective is the essential co-creator for any house capsule.

people.name: Chance the Rapper
people.role: Rapper from West Chatham and founder of SocialWorks
people.why: A YOUmedia alumnus and lifelong Chicago booster who headlined the 2020 All-Star halftime show at the United Center, and the most recognizable bridge between the scene and the arena.

people.name: Common
people.role: South Side rapper and actor; Grammy and Oscar winner
people.why: The son of an ABA player, he gave the spoken-word player intros at the 2020 All-Star Game and is the elder statesman of Chicago's conscious, wordplay-first lineage.

people.name: Saba (Pivot Gang)
people.role: Rapper and producer from Austin on the West Side
people.why: He comes from the United Center's side of town; 'Care for Me' and his recent work with producer No I.D. make him the respected local voice of the current era.

people.name: Ravyn Lenae
people.role: South Side R&B singer and Chicago High School for the Arts alumna
people.why: 'Love Me Not' made her one of the city's biggest breakout stars of 2025, a rising, non-drill face who reaches young fans.

people.name: Teklife
people.role: Footwork crew and label founded by DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn
people.why: Keepers of footwork since Rashad's death in 2014, they are the right partners for dance-led sneaker content.

people.name: Honey Dijon
people.role: Chicago-raised (born in Newark) house DJ, producer and fashion designer
people.why: She won a Grammy as a producer on Beyoncé's 'Renaissance' and has collaborated with Comme des Garçons, which makes her the scene's proven bridge from house to fashion.

people.name: Brandon Breaux
people.why: He made the artwork for Chance's 'Acid Rap,' the defining album art of Chicago's 2010s rap wave, and would be a natural illustrator for a Bulls city collection.

vocabulary.meaning: The dance music named for The Warehouse; a 'house head' is a lifelong devotee, often of the picnic-going generation.
The original house dance and its verb, a full-body pulse to the beat, as in Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body.'
The fast South and West Side dance-battle style and its 160-BPM music; 'juke' is the earlier party sound it grew out of.
Chicago-style stepping, a smooth partner dance done at steppers' sets in Black adult lounges and set to classic R&B.
WBMX's Hot Mix 5 radio mixes of the 1980s, taped off the air onto cassettes and passed around; shorthand for old-school Chicago mixing.
The stretch of South Michigan Avenue where Chess, Vee-Jay and other labels pressed Chicago blues, soul and doo-wop in the 1950s and '60s.
Chicago Stadium, the Bulls' Jordan-era home across Madison Street from the United Center, famous for crowd noise and its thundering Barton pipe organ.
The Chicago-born street-rap style; recognize its slang and set references so you can keep them off product.

designCues.cue: Spotlight red on blackout: Bulls red caught in a single roving beam against a darkened arena, straight from the lights-out intro
designCues.source: The Bulls' 'Sirius' starting-lineup intro, from Chicago Stadium to the United Center
designCues.use: Print reflective or glow spotlight beams in Bulls red on near-black (#0B0B0B) warmups so they flare under the intro lights; no song name or lyric needed.

designCues.cue: House-flag light blue: the Chicago flag's sky blue as reworked on house-music picnic tees
designCues.source: Chicago-flag 'House Music' tees worn at the Chosen Few Picnic and around the house scene
designCues.use: Use as the base for a house capsule, with red six-point stars (#FF0000) reworked as record centers; co-design with house DJs rather than copying fan bootlegs.

designCues.cue: Uptown neon green: the glowing tube script of the city's old music-room signs
designCues.source: The Green Mill's neon sign and the neon signage of South and North Side blues clubs
designCues.use: Use as a small accent of neon-tube embroidered script on a heritage blues and jazz capsule; spell out original words only and never copy club marks without permission.

designCues.source: Photocopied flyers for The Warehouse, the Music Box and Hot Mix 5 parties
designCues.use: Set pregame-tee graphics in this style for Bulls home dates, with art direction by Chicago designers and credit to the flyer archivists the team draws from.

designCues.use: Use for a rebuild-era tee or hangtag, and pair it with a real mix by a local DJ released as launch content.

designCues.use: Use as a print for insoles, socks and shorts on a footwork-tested low-top, built with paid Teklife and footwork crew input.

productHooks: 'Born in Chicago' house capsule: a Bulls pregame shooting shirt and tee in house-flag blue with Warehouse-flyer type, co-designed with and paying the Chosen Few DJs, released at the July picnic and restocked on Frankie Knuckles Day (Aug. 25).
Lights-out 'Spotlight' warmup: a near-black jacket with reflective Bulls-red beam graphics that flare during the United Center intro, launched at the 2026-27 home opener.
Footwork-tested low-top: a Nike Basketball low in Bulls colors, wear-tested and launched by Teklife and footwork crews at a South or West Side battle, with a rhythm-grid insole.
'Rebuild Mixtape' tee: Giddey, Buzelis, Wilson, Powell and Claxton as a cassette tracklist, sold with a mix by a Chicago DJ and a halftime set at the United Center.

Record Row heritage capsule, released for the June Blues Fest: a vintage-wash tee and coaches jacket with original label-style graphics and neon-script accents, with proceeds shared with Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation.
City-pack copy and art from the open-mic pipeline: commission Young Chicago Authors and YOUmedia poets to write the copy and Brandon Breaux to illustrate it, with a spoken-word halftime moment.
watchouts: Drill is tied to real killings and active feuds, and Lil Durk was federally charged with murder-for-hire in 2024 (case status unverified), so keep drill slang, set and block references (O-Block, 'on foenem,' 'Chiraq') and its artists off product and out of content.

R. Kelly, who is convicted and wrote 'I Believe I Can Fly' for Space Jam, and Kanye West, after his antisemitic statements and the adidas split, are off-limits, including in Jordan-era nostalgia, playlists and archival footage.

Licensing: 'Sirius' is Alan Parsons Project IP and 'Sirius' is also a SiriusXM mark. Chess, Trax and Dance Mania label art, the band Chicago's logo, Lyrical Lemonade branding and Frankie Knuckles' name and likeness all need clearance, so design originals or license.

House was built by Black and Latino queer DJs and dancers at The Warehouse. Telling it as a generic 'Chicago party' erases them, so credit and pay Black and queer DJs, consult the Knuckles estate and the Chosen Few, and don't limit it to Pride-month timing.
Check rival-brand deals before any partnership: Derrick Rose, Englewood's hometown hero, is a longtime adidas athlete, and artist footwear and apparel deals change fast.

art.headline: Chicago brands itself with civic graphics (flag stars, CTA line colors, grid-numbered street signs) and painted the country's first community mural, the Wall of Respect. In a rebuild year Nike should commission from that tradition rather than recycle the '90s.
art.summary: Chicago's look is civic and systematic. The 1917 flag maps the North, West and South Sides in pale blue and white. Street signs print each block's grid number, CTA L lines go by color, and Louis Sullivan's cast-iron ornament marks State and Madison, the point the address grid counts from. Its walls carry the country's deepest community-mural lineage: OBAC's 1967 Wall of Respect in Bronzeville, AfriCOBRA's 'Kool-Aid colors', Pilsen's Mexican muralism and the steel Puerto Rican flags on Paseo Boricua. Chicago also has its own pop art in the Hairy Who and the Imagists, and a streetwear lineage that runs from RSVP Gallery to Jordan Brand. With a new regime (coach Tiago Splitter, EVP Bryson Graham) building around Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson, the opening is to keep the unchanged 1966 bull as the constant and let living Chicago artists draw the new era.

insights.title: Chicago invented the community mural
insights.detail: In 1967 the Organization of Black American Culture's visual artists painted the Wall of Respect at 43rd and Langley in Bronzeville, a 'heroes' wall with a sports panel beside its jazz, literature and statesmen sections. It started the community-mural movement, which led to William Walker and John Pitman Weber's Chicago Mural Group (later Chicago Public Art Group) in 1971.
insights.implication: In Chicago a mural is a neighborhood-owned civic statement, not an ad wall. Any Bulls or Nike mural should be commissioned from South and West Side muralists, credited by name, and can openly cite the Wall of Respect lineage.

insights.title: AfriCOBRA made Chicago art wearable
insights.detail: AfriCOBRA, founded on the South Side in 1968 by Jeff Donaldson, Wadsworth Jarrell, Jae Jarrell, Barbara Jones-Hogu and Gerald Williams, wrote a visual code: 'Kool-Aid colors', shine, free symmetry, and lettering woven into the figures. Jae Jarrell's 'Revolutionary Suit' made it literal clothing.
insights.implication: No other NBA city has an art movement this native to apparel. Build Black History Month product on AfriCOBRA principles through licensed work with surviving members and estates, not generic Pan-African graphics.

insights.title: The city's civic graphics already work as fan gear
insights.detail: The flag's four six-pointed stars are probably the city's most common tattoo, and its three white bands stand for the North, West and South Sides. Street signs carry the grid number (Halsted 800 W, Ashland 1600 W, Damen 2000 W), honorary street signs are brown, and even the city vehicle sticker has been designed by high-school students through the City Clerk's contest.
insights.implication: Fans already treat municipal design as identity, but flag tees are everywhere. The less-used codes (grid numbers, brown honorary signs, the L palette, Sullivan ornament) are the open territory for City Edition and capsule work.

insights.title: Pilsen and Humboldt Park paint in their own idiom
insights.detail: Pilsen's walls, from the 16th Street rail embankment to Hector Duarte's studio mural, carry Mexican muralism, anchored by the National Museum of Mexican Art's Día de Muertos exhibition. On Division Street two 1995 steel Puerto Rican flags mark Paseo Boricua. Pilsen also remembers fights over the protection of older murals such as Casa Aztlán's.
insights.implication: Latino fan product must be authored by these communities (commissioned, paid, credited, launched in the neighborhood) and must avoid gentrification optics. A brand mural that overwrites local work would be a crisis.

insights.title: Chicago's streetwear bench is split between Nike and its competitors
insights.detail: Don C and Virgil Abloh opened RSVP Gallery in Wicker Park in 2009. Don C went on to Jordan Brand collaborations (the Air Jordan 2 'Just Don', the Legacy 312), and the MCA debuted Abloh's 'Figures of Speech' in 2019. Joe Freshgoods, the city's most-followed current streetwear voice, makes his Chicago-story releases with New Balance.
insights.implication: Nike's Chicago credibility runs through Jordan Brand, but the next bench is open. Scout SAIC fashion students and the Columbia College and Wabash Arts Corridor scene rather than chasing a competitor's partner.

insights.title: Chicago has its own pop art: the Imagists
insights.detail: The Hairy Who (Jim Nutt, Gladys Nilsson, Karl Wirsum, Suellen Rocca, Art Green, James Falconer) showed at the Hyde Park Art Center from 1966 to 1969. Their crude comic-book line and carnival color, along with Ed Paschke's neon-drenched portraits, are the city's homegrown visual dialect.
insights.implication: Imagism is a Chicago-only alternative to generic graffiti graphics and suits a young, gangly, physical 'SLAP' roster. License estates or brief living artists in the idiom, ideally through the Hyde Park Art Center.

insights.title: A logo that never changed and a statue that never left
insights.detail: The charging-bull mark, credited to Chicago commercial artist Dean Wessel in 1966, has never been redesigned. 'The Spirit', the 1994 Jordan statue by Omri Amrany and Julie Rotblatt-Amrany from their Highland Park studio, still anchors the United Center.
insights.implication: Keep the bull as the fixed point and let new Chicago art carry the Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson era. Fans will read another '90s throwback cycle in a rebuild year as filler.

vocabulary.meaning: The CTA's elevated and subway rail. The Loop is named for the ring of track around downtown, and lines are known by color (Red, Blue, Brown, Green, Orange, Pink, Purple, Yellow).

vocabulary.term: The four stars / the fifth star
vocabulary.meaning: The flag's stars mark Fort Dearborn, the 1871 Fire, the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition and the 1933 Century of Progress; Chicagoans periodically campaign for a fifth.
The zero point of the address grid. Every address counts out from here at about 800 numbers per mile, so locals give directions by number ('it's at 2400 West').
Area-code shorthand: 312 is downtown, 773 is the neighborhoods. Both are worn as identity, as in Jordan Brand's Legacy 312.
The city's signature housing: brick two-unit buildings and limestone-faced greystones lining neighborhood blocks.
The winter custom of saving a shoveled parking spot with a lawn chair, cone or laundry basket. It's beloved and argued over, and it coincides with basketball season.
AfriCOBRA's name for its saturated, luminous palette, one of the movement's founding principles.
Chicago's 1960s-70s homegrown pop: comic-strip line, grotesque humor and loud color, as distinct from New York Pop Art.

designCues.cue: Flag Blue: the pale lake-and-river blue of the 1917 Chicago flag, set against Bulls red #CE1141 and black.
designCues.source: Wallace Rice's municipal flag. The two blue stripes are Lake Michigan and the North Branch, and the South Branch and canal. The three white bands are the North, West and South Sides.
designCues.use: Use it in the flag's proportions, as twin pinstripes on side panels, waistbands or collar tape. Avoid full-flag prints, which every bootleg tee already uses.

designCues.cue: The Chicago star: a six-pointed red star with long, narrow points, used singly or as a row of four.
designCues.source: The flag's stars, each marking a civic milestone. Fans already connect six points with six championships.
designCues.use: One star as a jock-tag or waistband medallion carrying a 'six points' championship story. Keep the flag's exact star geometry and never add a fifth star for a rebuilding team.

designCues.cue: The L palette: Red #C60C30, Blue #00A1DE, Brown #62361B, Green #009B3A, Orange #F9461C, Pink #E27EA6, Purple #522398, Yellow #F9E300.
designCues.source: CTA rail line colors, which riders read as neighborhood identity. The Red Line runs from Howard on the North Side to 95th on the South Side.
designCues.use: Use the colors as a stripe system or a line-per-colorway series, with terminal-stop names as the type. CTA signage and marks need a license.

designCues.cue: Street-sign typography: white condensed sans on green with the hundred-block grid number in the corner, plus the brown signs used for honorary streets.
designCues.source: Chicago street-name signs, which carry grid coordinates (Madison 0 N/S, Damen 2000 W) and set the city's everyday lettering.
designCues.use: Build a number and wordmark lockup around '1901 W Madison', the United Center's address. Use brown 'honorary' signs to salute legends on tees and neck tape.

designCues.cue: Sullivan ornament: interlaced foliage and geometric cast-iron scrollwork.
designCues.source: Louis Sullivan's corner rotunda at the Sullivan Center (State and Madison) and the Auditorium Building. Chicago School architecture is the city's design signature.
designCues.use: Use as a tonal jacquard, debossed trim or knit pattern in black-on-black or red-on-red. The buildings are public, but redraw the pattern rather than scanning photographs.

designCues.cue: AfriCOBRA code: saturated 'Kool-Aid' color, light-catching shine, and words built into the figures.
designCues.source: The South Side collective founded in 1968, extending the Wall of Respect's heroes tradition.
designCues.use: Use for Black History Month graphics with lettering integrated into player and fan imagery. Commission or license through AfriCOBRA members and estates, with credit and pay.

designCues.cue: Marquee and neon lettering: stacked vertical letters with bulb-dot and neon-tube outlines.
designCues.source: The Chicago Theatre's vertical 'CHICAGO' sign on State Street, the Green Mill's neon in Uptown and Superdawg's rooftop figures in Norwood Park.
designCues.use: Use a vertical 'CHICAGO' stack down a sleeve or side panel with a bulb-dot texture. Draw original letterforms and do not copy the theatre's trademarked sign.

designCues.cue: L steel and common brick: riveted girder grids and the irregular salmon-to-buff Chicago common brick of two-flats.
designCues.source: The Loop's 1890s elevated structure and the bungalow-belt and two-flat blocks.
designCues.use: Use a rivet-grid emboss on taping and outerwear yokes, and a tonal brick-bond jacquard on fleece, for winter product that feels like a Chicago block.

productHooks: '1901 W' grid pack: shooting shirt, hoodie and cap set in Chicago street-sign type (white on green), with Flag Blue pinstripes and each player's number shown as a grid coordinate. Commission the lettering from a Chicago type designer.

Wall of Respect / AfriCOBRA Black History Month capsule, licensed from members and estates in 'Kool-Aid' color with integrated lettering. Launch at the South Side Community Art Center and share proceeds with it.

'Ride the L' series: eight colorways of tees and crew socks under a CTA license, one per line, with terminal stops as typography. Lead with the Red Line (Howard to 95th) as the North-to-South Bulls unifier.

Noche Latina drop around Día de Muertos, commissioned from a Pilsen muralist such as Hector Duarte with the National Museum of Mexican Art and released in Pilsen. Use original artwork, not stock calaveras.
New-era wall: an artist-led mural of Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson on the Wabash Arts Corridor, unveiled on Open House Chicago weekend, with a limited print-and-tee run credited to the muralist.
watchouts: Brand conflicts: Joe Freshgoods works with New Balance, and Virgil Abloh's legacy is managed by his estate and the brands he led. Check exclusivity before approaching any Chicago designer, and avoid 'poaching' optics.

Third-party IP: CTA marks and signage, the Chicago Theatre sign, Morton Salt's umbrella girl, Vienna Beef and the Wrigley Field marquee (a Cubs asset) all need licenses or a full redraw. 'The Spirit' carries the sculptors' copyright plus Jordan's likeness.

Community authorship: Pilsen's murals, Día de Muertos ofrendas and calaveras, Mexica and Indigenous imagery, and the Puerto Rican flag are not decoration. Commission, credit and pay artists from those communities, and never paint over or crowd out existing murals; Casa Aztlán is still remembered.
Don't use 'Chiraq', drill-scene shorthand or violence tropes, and don't show the South and West Sides only through hardship. Use their artists, institutions and joy.
The flag and four stars are saturated in bootleg merch and carry specific civic meanings. Execute them precisely, and never invent a fifth star to manufacture hype for a rebuilding team.

food.headline: Chicago eats standing at the counter, with beef ordered 'dipped, hot,' dogs 'dragged through the garden' with no ketchup and pizza tavern-cut into squares, and the Chicago dog's tomato and poppy seed already match Bulls red and black.
food.summary: Chicago's food identity is working-class, neighborhood-owned and eaten fast: Italian beef from Al's #1 and Johnnie's, Chicago dogs from Superdawg and Gene & Jude's, tavern-cut pizza on the Southwest Side, and a Black-owned South Side canon of Harold's, Lem's rib tips and mild sauce. Its immigrant corridors (Pilsen and Little Village, the jibarito on Paseo Boricua, Devon Avenue, Polish Milwaukee Avenue) give each side of town its own menu. Bulls game day is a pre-game dinner in the triangle of Randolph Street, Greektown and Taylor Street, not a tailgate. In a rebuild year under Tiago Splitter, with Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and Caleb Wilson, food is a low-risk way for Nike to show neighborhood pride, provided it pays and credits the stands and licenses their marks.

insights.title: The Chicago dog already wears Bulls colors
insights.detail: A Chicago dog is an all-beef frank on a poppy-seed bun with yellow mustard, neon-green relish, onion, tomato wedges, a pickle spear, sport peppers and celery salt ('dragged through the garden'), and asking for ketchup gets you mocked. The stands locals defend are Superdawg (Norwood Park, 1948) and Gene & Jude's in River Grove, which piles fries on top and has no seats.
insights.implication: Tomato red and poppy-seed black are Bulls red and black, so a hot-dog accent pack (neon relish, mustard, seed speckle) reads as Chicago without any literal food graphic. 'No ketchup' is the insider joke a hangtag or insole can carry.

insights.title: Italian beef is ordered in code
insights.detail: At Al's #1 on Taylor Street (since 1938), Johnnie's in Elmwood Park and Mr. Beef on Orleans, you order 'sweet or hot' (roasted peppers or giardiniera), 'dry, juicy or dipped,' and 'combo' (beef plus sausage), then eat in 'the Italian stance,' leaning over the counter so the jus misses your shirt. FX's The Bear, modeled on Mr. Beef, took that vocabulary national.
insights.implication: The order code is a ready-made naming and colorway system (Dipped, Hot, Combo) for a fan pack, and beef-stand workwear cues (aprons, deli paper, order stamps) land right now. Draw from the real stands and pay them; The Bear's names and marks are FX/Disney IP.

insights.title: Locals eat tavern-cut, visitors eat deep dish
insights.detail: The everyday Chicago pizza is cracker-thin tavern-style cut into squares (the 'party cut'), from South Side spots like Vito & Nick's in Ashburn, and people fight over the crunchy corner pieces. Pequod's caramelized-crust pan pie is the cult exception, and food reporter Steve Dolinsky's book 'Pizza City, USA' argues that tavern style, not deep dish, is the city's real pie.
insights.implication: The square-cut grid is the insider pizza cue for watch-party product, while deep-dish graphics read as airport souvenirs. Tavern pizza is what Chicagoans eat during road games, so it suits a watch-party kit.

insights.title: The South Side canon is Black-owned and number-coded
insights.detail: Harold's Chicken Shack (founded 1950) is known by location number and served with mild sauce over fries and white bread. On 75th Street, Lem's Bar-B-Q smokes rib tips and hot links in a glass-walled 'aquarium' pit, and Brown Sugar Bakery down the block sells caramel cake; Erick Williams of Virtue in Hyde Park is the neighborhood's fine-dining voice.
insights.implication: This is the core of a February Black History Month food story, and it must be built as paid, credited partnerships with these owners, never by borrowing their logos or turning chicken and barbecue into a punchline.

insights.title: Immigrant corridors map the city
insights.detail: Pilsen's 18th Street (Carnitas Uruapan, since 1975) and Little Village's 26th Street anchor Mexican Chicago. The jibarito, a steak sandwich with fried plantains for bread, was created in Humboldt Park in 1996 and lives along Paseo Boricua; Patel Brothers opened its first store on Devon Avenue in 1974, and Polish bakeries line Milwaukee Avenue.
insights.implication: Co-design neighborhood capsules corridor by corridor with local businesses and cultural groups, timed to heritage nights and summer festivals, instead of one generic 'Chicago food' print.

insights.title: Game day is a pre-game dinner, not a tailgate
insights.detail: The United Center (1901 W. Madison) sits inside a food triangle: Randolph Street and Fulton Market a mile east (Au Cheval, Girl & the Goat), Greektown on Halsted, and Taylor Street's Little Italy, with Jim's Original Maxwell Street Polish stand near UIC. Winter means Bulls fans eat before tip-off instead of tailgating in the lots.
insights.implication: Stage launch-night activations indoors inside that triangle, such as a Fulton Market pop-up or collab wrappers at Al's on City Edition nights. Design for fans commuting in coats over jerseys on the No. 20 Madison bus or the L plus a long walk.

insights.title: The rebuild has a hometown pantry
insights.detail: Matas Buzelis is a Chicago-area native of Lithuanian heritage, and greater Chicago is home to one of the largest Lithuanian communities outside Lithuania, with dishes like cepelinai dumplings and spit-baked sakotis 'tree cake.' With the new Splitter-Graham regime starting over and expectations low, homegrown stories carry more than win totals.
insights.implication: A Buzelis-fronted community night with Lithuanian-American bakeries and organizations gives local fans a reason to buy in during a rebuild. Confirm his community ties and get their buy-in before concepting.

vocabulary.meaning: A Chicago dog with all seven toppings and celery salt, never ketchup.
Italian beef order: the whole sandwich dunked in jus, topped with hot giardiniera. 'Juicy' is a lighter dunk; 'sweet' means roasted green peppers.
Italian beef plus a char-grilled Italian sausage in the same roll.
Leaning over the counter, elbows out, so a dripping beef misses your clothes.
Oil-packed hot giardiniera, the city's all-purpose condiment on beef, pizza and eggs.
Thin-crust pizza cut into squares instead of wedges; the corner pieces are prized.
The sweet, tangy red sauce poured over wings and fries at South and West Side chicken shacks.
A Puerto Rican sandwich that uses flattened fried plantains as the bread, born in Humboldt Park.

culture.headline: Chicago is a city of sides with a Second City chip, and the Bulls play on Madison Street, the line where North and South Side addresses begin, which makes them the one team every side shares.
culture.summary: Chicago sees itself the way Carl Sandburg wrote it in 1914: 'City of the Big Shoulders', a working city that rebuilt itself after the 1871 fire and took the nickname 'Second City', first meant as an East Coast jab, as a badge. It assumes the rest of the country knows it as flyover country or as a crime talking point, and it bristles at both. Identity runs through sides (North, South, West, the suburbs), 77 community areas, parishes and high schools, and a population that is roughly one-third Black, one-third Latino and one-third white, built by the Great Migration and generations of immigrants. Daily life is shaped by winter and the Hawk, and the city's calendar fills with parades from Bud Billiken to the green river. Nike's opening in a rebuild year is to make product that unites the sides, rooted in civic symbols locals actually use, built for January walks to the United Center and co-authored with the communities that make the city what it is.

insights.title: Second City, Big Shoulders
insights.detail: Chicagoans see themselves as blunt, hardworking and unpretentious: Sandburg's 'Hog Butcher for the World', Richard J. Daley's 'The City That Works', and the 'I Will' motto from the 1890s, when the city rose from the Great Fire to win the 1893 World's Fair. A.J. Liebling's 1952 New Yorker put-down 'The Second City' became a comedy institution and a point of pride, and locals know 'Windy City' is usually explained as a dig at its boastful promoters, not its weather.
insights.implication: Write the product voice in a working-class, understated register: earned, durable and a little defiant, not flashy. Public-domain civic language like 'City of the Big Shoulders' and 'I Will' fits a rebuild built on size and physicality better than another '90s victory lap.

insights.title: Madison Street runs through the arena
insights.detail: The street grid starts at State and Madison: everything north of Madison is a North address and everything south is a South address, and the United Center sits at 1901 W. Madison on the Near West Side, across the street from where Chicago Stadium stood. Baseball splits the city (Cubs North Side, Sox South Side), but the Bulls draw from every side and the suburbs, and locals still size each other up by side, neighborhood and 'Where'd you go to high school?'
insights.implication: Treat the Bulls as Chicago's unifier. Build North/South/West/suburbs product that adds up to one city rather than pitting sides against each other, and use grid coordinates, community areas and high-school pride as hyperlocal hooks.

insights.title: A Black-founded, Great Migration city
insights.detail: Chicago's first non-Native settler, Jean Baptiste Point DuSable, was a Black trader widely described as Haitian-born; Lake Shore Drive was renamed for him in 2021. From about 1916 to 1970, Black Southerners, many from the Mississippi Delta, came north on the Illinois Central, encouraged by Robert S. Abbott's Chicago Defender, and built Bronzeville into the 'Black Metropolis' of Ida B. Wells, Gwendolyn Brooks, Harold Washington and Mamie Till-Mobley. Since 2000 many Black families have moved to the 708 south suburbs.
insights.implication: Black Chicago is the Bulls' cultural engine. Co-author heritage product with its institutions (DuSable Museum, Chicago Defender Charities, South Side designers), credit and pay them, and stock it in the south suburbs as well as downtown.

insights.title: La Villita, Pilsen and Paseo Boricua under pressure
insights.detail: Latino Chicagoans are about 30 percent of the city (2020 Census), mostly Mexican in Pilsen and Little Village and Puerto Rican in Humboldt Park, whose activism goes back to the 1966 Division Street uprising. In fall 2025 a federal immigration enforcement surge centered on these neighborhoods, and residents organized rapid-response networks, including whistles to warn neighbors.
insights.implication: Latino fans are a core Bulls market, but 2026-27 activations must be bilingual, community-led and physically safe: partner with local designers and institutions such as the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts & Culture, and never collect data, film residents or borrow protest imagery.

insights.title: Chicago grows the stars other cities win with
insights.detail: Chicago-area hoopers keep winning titles elsewhere: Isiah Thomas (West Side) with Detroit, Kevin Garnett (Farragut) with Boston, Dwyane Wade (Richards HS) with Miami, Anthony Davis (Englewood) with the Lakers, and in June 2026 Jalen Brunson (Stevenson HS, Lincolnshire) as Finals MVP for the Knicks. Derrick Rose, the Englewood and Simeon kid who became the 2011 MVP for his hometown team, is still the city's model of a homegrown star, and Simeon's No. 25 for Ben Wilson, killed in 1984, is Public League scripture.
insights.implication: Tell Chicago-made basketball stories (the Public League, Simeon, the Catholic League, park leagues) as the city's own heritage, then hand that pride to the Splitter-era core of Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson. Partner with the schools and families instead of taking their numbers and names.

insights.title: The home season is Hawk season
insights.detail: The NBA season runs through the months when 'the Hawk', the wind off Lake Michigan, makes 20 degrees feel like zero; the January 2019 polar vortex hit about -23F. Fans reach the United Center by the No. 20 Madison bus or a long walk from the nearest L stops, so the real fan uniform is a long parka, a knit hat and a hoodie under it, and summer is lived outside on the 18-mile lakefront.
insights.implication: Make outerwear the hero of Chicago game-day product: wind-blocking stadium parkas, heavyweight fleece, cuffed knits and gloves, with reflective details for dark walks, timed to drop before the first freeze. Pivot to lakefront-weight tees and shorts for the spring and summer parade season.

insights.title: Dynasty pride, ownership fatigue
insights.detail: The six titles (1991-93, 1996-98) and their Grant Park rallies are the city's last great shared sports celebration, and June 13, 2027 marks 30 years since Steve Kerr's title-clinching shot on Jordan's pass. Local pride now coexists with a 31-51 season and long frustration with the Reinsdorf era, which surfaced in booing during the January 2024 Ring of Honor ceremony.
insights.implication: Use the '90s through Jordan Brand with restraint and pair every legacy piece with the new core, so heritage feels like a promise rather than a substitute. Fan-made language beats official 'loyalty' messaging, which can read as tone-deaf in a rebuild.

places.name: State and Madison
places.why: The zero point of the address grid, once billed as 'the World's Busiest Corner': Madison divides North from South and State divides East from West, so every Chicago address counts from here.

places.name: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center
places.why: Founded in 1961 by artist-educator Margaret Burroughs, it is one of the oldest independent Black history museums in the U.S. and the natural co-author for Black heritage stories.

places.name: Pullman National Historical Park and A. Philip Randolph Pullman Porter Museum
places.why: The company town, the 1894 strike and the Pullman porters' union tell the labor and Black history behind 'The City That Works'.

places.name: Little Village Arch ('Bienvenidos a Little Village')
places.why: The gateway to 26th Street, the Mexican commercial corridor often cited (unverified) as the city's second-busiest shopping strip after Michigan Avenue.

places.name: National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts & Culture
places.why: Housed in the park's historic stables near Paseo Boricua, it anchors Puerto Rican Chicago's cultural memory.

places.name: American Indian Center of Chicago
places.why: Founded in 1953, it is one of the oldest urban Native centers in the country and the right first call before any Native-related story or land acknowledgment.

places.name: Chicago History Museum
places.why: The city's archive from the Great Fire to the Bulls dynasty, and a credible partner for heritage capsules and archival graphics.

places.name: Promontory Point
places.why: A limestone-stepped peninsula where South Siders swim and watch the skyline, and a neighborhood-defended symbol of public lakefront access.

places.name: Al's #1 Italian Beef
places.why: Open since 1938 and the best place to learn the beef vocabulary (dipped, hot, sweet) every Chicagoan speaks.

places.name: Superdawg Drive-In
places.why: A 1948 Milwaukee Avenue drive-in with Maurie and Flaurie, the giant hot dog figures on the roof; a Northwest Side landmark of the city's hot dog culture.

people.name: Michael Jordan
people.why: A North Carolinian whom Chicago adopted; his statue 'The Spirit' and the six titles are the city's global calling card, available to Nike through Jordan Brand.

people.name: Derrick Rose
people.role: Englewood native, Simeon alum, 2011 NBA MVP
people.why: The hometown kid who became the league's youngest MVP is the most loved local Bull and the model of the homegrown star Chicago wants back.

people.name: Dwyane Wade
people.role: Hall of Famer, South Side native
people.why: A Richards High School product who won three titles in Miami and came home to play for the Bulls in 2016-17, so he embodies both Chicago's hoops pipeline and its pull.

people.name: Stacey King
people.role: Bulls TV analyst and '90s Bulls champion
people.why: His calls ('Gimme the hot sauce!', 'Kaboom!') are part of how local fans talk about the team.

people.name: Benny the Bull
people.why: Older than the dynasty and loved across generations, he is a ready-made character for kids' and family product.

people.name: Lena Waithe
people.role: Writer and producer, South Side native
people.why: She created Showtime's 'The Chi', which showed South Side family life to a national audience on its own terms.

people.name: The Second City
people.role: Improv theater in Old Town, founded 1959
people.why: It turned the city's 'Second City' put-down into a world-famous institution, the clearest example of Chicago owning its chip.

people.name: Chicago Defender Charities
people.role: Organizer of the Bud Billiken Parade
people.why: It carries the Chicago Defender's Great Migration legacy into the largest African American parade in the country.

moments.name: Bud Billiken Parade and Picnic
moments.why: Founded in 1929 by the Chicago Defender, this back-to-school parade down King Drive to Washington Park is the South Side's biggest day of the year.

moments.name: Mexican Independence Day Parade on 26th Street
moments.why: Little Village and Pilsen fill with flags, banda and lowriders, the clearest public expression of Mexican Chicago pride.

moments.name: Chinatown Lunar New Year Parade
moments.timing: Early-to-mid February (Lunar New Year is Feb. 6, 2027, Year of the Goat)
moments.why: Chinatown's in-season parade on Wentworth Avenue is a February moment for Chicago's Chinese American community.

moments.name: Chicago's birthday
moments.why: The city was incorporated on March 4, 1837; the 190th birthday falls mid-season and gives a natural hook for civic-symbol product.

moments.name: St. Patrick's river dyeing, parade and South Side Irish Parade
moments.timing: Saturday before March 17 (expected March 13, 2027), Beverly's parade that Sunday
moments.why: Plumbers Local 130 has dyed the Chicago River green since 1962, and Bridgeport and Beverly carry the Irish South Side identity.

moments.name: Puerto Rican Fest and People's Parade
moments.why: Humboldt Park and Paseo Boricua's flag-filled week of pride.

moments.name: Chicago Pride Parade
moments.why: One of the largest Pride parades in the U.S., running through Lakeview and Northalsted.

moments.name: 30th anniversary of the 1997 title
moments.why: Thirty years since Kerr's shot clinched title No. 5 at the United Center, landing during the playoffs as a heritage beat.

designCues.source: Chicago's address grid, which counts every address from State and Madison at 800 numbers to the mile.

designCues.cue: The municipal 'Y' device: a three-pronged Y standing for the Chicago River's main stem and its North and South branches.
designCues.source: The city symbol cast on bridges, park buildings and older municipal structures.
designCues.use: A small hidden mark (jock tag, waistband, knit-cuff patch) that locals will spot. Confirm the City's usage rules first.

designCues.cue: 'I Will' and 'City of the Big Shoulders' set in heavy condensed industrial capitals, like stencils on rail cars and grain elevators.
designCues.source: The 1890s civic motto and Carl Sandburg's 1914 poem 'Chicago' (public domain).
designCues.use: Interior prints and shooting-shirt backs for the rebuild, giving the new size-and-physicality identity a civic voice.

designCues.cue: Area-code numerals 312, 773, 708, 630 and 847, set in Bulls-style block numbers.
designCues.source: 312 was the city's original code, 773 has covered the neighborhoods since 1996, and 708, 630 and 847 cover the suburbs where much of the fan base lives.
designCues.use: Side and suburb editions that sell where people live, from the south suburbs (708) to the North Shore (847).

designCues.cue: Water Tower limestone: the pale yellow-cream of the Joliet limestone Water Tower, one of the few buildings to survive the 1871 fire.
designCues.source: The 1869 Chicago Water Tower on Michigan Avenue, the city's symbol of survival and rebuilding.
designCues.use: A heritage base or tonal ground for 'I Will' pieces, under Bulls red and black.

designCues.source: The view along the lakefront and Lake Shore Drive from December through February.
designCues.use: A base color for Hawk-season outerwear and fleece, set against Bulls red trims.

designCues.cue: Mild sauce red-orange: the sweet, tangy sauce on wings and fish at South and West Side chicken and fish shacks.
designCues.source: Black-owned neighborhood spots such as Harold's Chicken Shack and countless wing joints.
designCues.use: A secondary accent for a food-culture capsule, made only in partnership with named local businesses that are credited and paid.

designCues.cue: The Hawk-season stadium parka: knee-length, wind-blocking, with a hood cut to fit over a fitted cap, storm cuffs and reflective piping.
designCues.source: Fans walking from the L or the Madison bus to the United Center in January.
designCues.use: The hero Chicago game-day piece, in Bulls black with lake-gray lining and red reflective details.

productHooks: 'Madison Street' collection: split North/South hoodies and tees carrying the 0/0 grid coordinate and 1901 W. Madison, sold at the United Center and at shops on all sides of the city as a one-city statement.
'Hawk Season' outerwear drop before the first freeze in November: stadium parka, heavyweight fleece and a cuffed knit hat with a hidden Y-device patch, built for the walk from the bus or L.
A Chicago-first 'Gym Shoes' basketball footwear pack and campaign that uses the local word, launched through Public League and park-league programs rather than downtown retail alone.
'I Will' shooting shirts and tees for the young Splitter-era core (Giddey, Buzelis, Caleb Wilson), with Sandburg lines printed inside, released around Chicago's 190th birthday on March 4, 2027.

Neighborhood editions for the 77 community areas, co-designed and paid with local creatives in places such as Bronzeville, Little Village, Humboldt Park and Chatham, with bilingual tags where it fits.
A Bud Billiken back-to-school kids' collection (August 2027) made with Chicago Defender Charities, pairing Benny the Bull gear with gym shoes and giving back to South Side schools.
watchouts: Never use 'Chiraq', crime-tape or bullet imagery, or drill-scene and gang-linked slang. These tie to real deaths, and Chicagoans resent being used as a national crime talking point.

Latino neighborhoods have lived under federal immigration enforcement since fall 2025. Activations there must be community-led and bilingual, must not collect data or film residents, and must not borrow protest symbols such as whistles.

Chicago is Council of Three Fires (Potawatomi, Odawa, Ojibwe) homeland, and the name comes from a Native word for wild onion. The Blackhawks, who share the United Center, carry a long logo controversy, so keep all Native imagery off Bulls product and consult the American Indian Center for anything Native-related.

License or clear third-party IP: City of Chicago symbols (flag, seal, Y device), Bud Billiken and Chicago Defender marks, restaurant names (Harold's, Al's, Superdawg), FX's 'The Bear', and Cubs, Sox and Bears marks, which cannot appear on Bulls product. Jordan's name and likeness go through Jordan Brand.

Stay out of politics and ownership fights: Chicago holds municipal elections in February-April 2027, fans are frustrated with the Reinsdorf era, Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV is a point of pride that should never be commercialized, and figures like Kanye West and R. Kelly are off-limits.

underground.headline: Chicago's underground runs on things the city invented (JB rink skating, the pinball and arcade cabinet, a sneaker colorway named after the Bulls) and on thrift racks still full of six titles' worth of gear, which gives a rebuild with no superstar credible lanes far from drill and the street.
underground.summary: Chicago's scenes are inventions, not imports. South Side skaters roll in synchronized JB 'trains' at The Rink on East 87th Street, Chicago companies from Bally and Williams to Midway built the pinball machine and the arcade basketball game (NBA Jam, whose Bulls famously had no Jordan), and the Air Jordan 1 made the Bulls' home whites a sneaker word worldwide, served today by boutiques like Notre and RSVP Gallery. The dynasty also filled the thrift racks with Starter pullovers, Champion jerseys and bootleg title tees, feeding a strict vintage culture and a newer rework scene. What is rising in 2025-26 is the scenes that never needed a superstar: JB skating clips spreading on social, pinball and arcade bars, covered skateparks like Logan Boulevard's under the Kennedy, and a Black queer nightlife lineage on the South Side that predates Northalsted's rainbow. Nike can engage rink, arcade, skate, vintage and queer nightlife through paid, credited partners, and should leave drill, gang-nation symbols and street takeovers alone.

insights.title: The team's home whites became a sneaker word
insights.detail: Since 1985 sneakerheads worldwide have called the white, red and black Air Jordan 1 'Chicagos,' and Chicagoans still say 'gym shoes' for any sneaker. The boutique tier (Notre in the West Loop, RSVP Gallery (Saint Alfred closed its Wicker Park store in April 2026)) sells to the most Jordan-saturated customers anywhere.
insights.implication: One more white-red-black 'Chicago' colorway is the one thing this market already owns. Nike Basketball's Bulls product should bring new stories and materials, coordinate with Jordan Brand, and route boutique collaborations through partners with Nike history like Notre.

insights.title: Chicago built the arcade, and NBA Jam's Bulls had no Jordan
insights.detail: Bally, Williams, Gottlieb and Midway made Chicago the capital of pinball and arcade games, and Stern Pinball in Elk Grove Village is still the world's largest pinball maker. Midway made NBA Jam (1993) in Chicago without Jordan, who controlled his own likeness, so its Bulls were Scottie Pippen and Horace Grant; lead designer Mark Turmell, a Pistons fan, later admitted coding the Bulls to miss late shots against Detroit.
insights.implication: Dot-matrix numerals, backglass art and 'heating up' flames give the Bulls a story that needs no superstar, which suits the Giddey-Buzelis-Wilson rebuild. Evoke the language in original art and license any NBA Jam names, sounds or catchphrases.

insights.title: JB skating is the South Side's rink language
insights.detail: Chicago's own rhythm roller-skating style, JB (after James Brown's funk), moves in synchronized 'trains' of skaters doing smooth backward footwork to a mid-tempo groove, and The Rink on East 87th Street is its home floor. Crews dress alike in track suits and custom tees, and the 2020s roller boom carried JB clips far beyond the South Side.
insights.implication: A Bulls track suit cut for skating, co-designed with JB crews who are credited and paid and launched at the rink rather than downtown, would reach a style-setting Black Chicago community that no other market has.

insights.title: Six titles flooded the thrift racks
insights.detail: The 1991-98 dynasty left Chicago full of Starter half-zip pullovers, Champion jerseys, Chalk Line jackets and bootleg 'three-peat' tees, which still surface at Village Discount Outlet, the Maxwell Street Market and Milwaukee Ave vintage shops. Younger Chicagoans now cut and re-sew these pieces into patchwork jackets and reworked hoodies.
insights.implication: Vintage Bulls is the city's thrift currency, so reissues must be archive-exact down to the tag. 'Three-Peat' is Pat Riley's trademark and retired players need licensing, so original silhouettes in aged color are safer than copying old graphics.

insights.title: Skaters won sanctioned concrete, but winter still rules
insights.detail: Chicago skaters now have Park District parks on the lakefront (Wilson in Uptown, Grant in the South Loop) and the skater-backed Logan Boulevard park under the Kennedy Expressway, which stays dry in rain. Uprise Skateshop on Milwaukee Ave anchors the scene, and months of 'Chiberia' push sessions under overpasses and indoors.
insights.implication: A Nike SB x Bulls drop is credible only through local shops and skaters, with money for park upkeep, and it has to be built for Chicago cold: wind-blocking shells, brushed fleece and gloves that keep grip.

insights.title: Queer nightlife runs from Northalsted to South Shore
insights.detail: The North Side's Northalsted strip (renamed from Boystown in 2022) hosts Pride in June and Market Days in August. The city's Black queer lineage, which gave house music its first floor at The Warehouse, lives on in South Side rooms like South Shore's Jeffery Pub and in Chicago's ballroom and kiki scene.
insights.implication: Pride and Market Days product co-designed with South Side Black queer creators and ballroom houses, credited and paid, with proceeds to an LGBTQ+ group they choose, avoids a generic North Side rainbow drop.

designCues.cue: Dot-matrix display amber
designCues.source: Orange plasma dot-matrix score displays on Bally, Williams and Stern pinball machines built in and around Chicago since the early 1990s.
designCues.use: A small accent for numbers and scores on black Bulls shooting shirts and hangtags, next to Bulls red (#CE1141), never a body color.

designCues.use: Garment-dyed fleece and tees in this red over a sail (#EFE6D3) base, against crisp Bulls red (#CE1141) on game product, so lifestyle reads 'found'.

designCues.source: The satin-and-nylon Bulls pullover with kangaroo pocket and side zip, the city's 1990s winter uniform and today's top vintage find.
designCues.use: Rebuild the silhouette in Nike's own construction (quilted lining, oversized hood, side zip) without Starter's star or other trade dress.

designCues.source: Unofficial dynasty-era championship tees: misregistered colors, slightly-off player art and heavy plastisol ink.
designCues.use: Apply the off-register look to original Bulls graphics on a limited lifestyle tee; never reproduce real bootleg art or 'three-peat' wording.

designCues.cue: Skate-train track suit
designCues.source: JB crews at The Rink on 87th dressing alike in fitted track suits for synchronized trains.
designCues.use: Smooth stretch tricot with a tapered, ankle-zip leg that clears skate boots and a blank chest panel for crew-name embroidery.

designCues.cue: The Bulls without Jordan, two-player mode
designCues.source: NBA Jam's 1993 Bulls were Pippen and Horace Grant because Jordan kept his likeness out of the game.
designCues.use: Frame rebuild duo product (Giddey and Buzelis, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson) as a two-player select screen: the Bulls have been cool without a superstar before.

productHooks: Bulls Arcade capsule: black shooting shirt and tee with original dot-grid numerals in display amber (#FF6B1A) and Bulls red (#CE1141), launched around Pinball Expo and the October tip-off at a Chicago arcade, with any NBA Jam references licensed first.
Two-Player Select tees: Giddey/Buzelis and Buzelis/Wilson duo graphics in an original 1990s select-screen layout under the NBPA group license, released for the first home game.

Rink Session track suit: a stretch tricot Bulls jacket and tapered ankle-zip pant cut for skating, co-designed with JB crews from The Rink on 87th, with custom crew-name embroidery and a South Side Bulls skate-night launch where crews are paid.

Basement Stock reissue: a Nike-built half-zip pullover and garment-dyed fleece in aged red (#A8323E) and sail (#EFE6D3), sold only at Chicago doors and the United Center as a nod to the city's thrift hunt.

Chiberia SB pack through Nike SB and Chicago skate shops: a wind-blocking Bulls shell, brushed fleece and grip gloves, with part of the proceeds going to upkeep at Logan Boulevard or Grant skatepark through a group the skaters choose.
Pride and Market Days warm-up co-designed with South Side Black queer creators and Chicago ballroom houses, with credited, paid partners and proceeds to an LGBTQ+ organization they pick.
watchouts: Jordan Brand owns the city's sneaker story: the 'Chicago' Air Jordan 1, the Jumpman and Jordan's name and likeness need Jordan Brand coordination, Virgil Abloh's designs belong to his estate and Off-White, and key locals have rival deals (Joe Freshgoods with New Balance, Angel Reese with Reebok (now traded from the Sky to Atlanta)).

Chicago street-gang 'nations' use specific symbols: pitchforks, crowns, five- and six-point stars combined with them, hat tilts and certain color pairings. Have local community partners review every graphic; the city flag's six-point stars are fine on their own.

Leave drill, O-Block and the word 'Chiraq' out entirely, along with street takeovers, drifting and dirt-bike or ATV stunts on Lake Shore Drive, which are illegal and a city enforcement priority. Downtown Mexican Independence Day car caravans have drawn police clashes.

Third-party IP: NBA Jam's name, sounds and catchphrases, pinball makers' marks (Stern, Bally, Williams), Starter's star, Pat Riley's 'Three-Peat' trademark and retired players' likenesses all need licensing.

JB skating, footwork, ballroom and South Side house nightlife are Black- and queer-built: partner with, credit and pay their crews and venues, and never brand non-commercial spaces like Critical Mass or skater-built spots.

hoops.headline: Chicago hoops is a Public League faith that claims players by high school and side of town (Simeon's Benji and Rose, Farragut's KG, Marshall's Hoop Dreams) and spends half the year in Park District fieldhouses because the Hawk shuts the outdoor courts.
hoops.summary: Chicago's basketball identity lives in the Chicago Public League (Simeon, Whitney Young, Farragut, Marshall, Morgan Park) and in suburban powers like Proviso East, and its canon is about loss and resilience, led by Simeon's Ben Wilson, the country's top high school player when he was killed in 1984. The game follows the weather: park and lakefront courts from May to September, Park District fieldhouses the rest of the year, and the season peaks in March when teams 'go downstate' for the IHSA finals, the tournament that gave basketball the phrase 'March Madness.' The market also has the WNBA's Chicago Sky, the G League's Windy City Bulls, DePaul and Loyola, and it hosts the NBA Draft Combine every May, so the hoops calendar never goes dark. Nike's opening is to build on what it already owns here (Mac Irvin Fire, the Bulls and Sky uniforms, the 'Chicago' color-blocking) in a city where many favorite sons, Derrick Rose first among them, wear rival brands.

insights.title: Claimed by school, then by side
insights.detail: Chicagoans introduce a player by high school before anything else: Simeon's Derrick Rose and Jabari Parker, Farragut's Kevin Garnett, Whitney Young's Quentin Richardson and Jahlil Okafor, Marshall's Cappie Pondexter and Patrick Beverley, Crane's Tony Allen, Proviso East's Doc Rivers and Michael Finley. Public League conferences are named by side of town (Red-South, Red-West), so a Simeon-Young city title game is also South Side against the Near West Side.
insights.implication: Make the school and the side the unit of storytelling: school-licensed shooting shirts and gym investments that name the program and the neighborhood, never a generic 'Chi-Town hooper.'

insights.title: Benji and No. 25 are sacred
insights.detail: Simeon's Ben Wilson was the nation's top-ranked high school player when he was shot near the school in November 1984, days before his senior season. His Simeon teammate Nick Anderson wore No. 25 at Illinois and in Orlando for him, and Derrick Rose wore it at Simeon. The city's hoops memory also holds near-misses like Farragut dunker Ronnie Fields.
insights.implication: Nike's role is to fund and amplify (Simeon's program, family-approved youth work), never to print 25 or the tragedy on product. Lead with resilience stories the people involved tell themselves.

insights.title: Fieldhouse city: the Hawk sends the game indoors
insights.detail: In 1905 the South Park Commission opened neighborhood parks with fieldhouses by D.H. Burnham & Co. and the Olmsted Brothers, a model copied across the country, and Park District fieldhouse gyms still carry winter leagues and open runs. Outdoor park and lakefront courts only really run from May to September, and spring and fall runs are played in hoodies under jerseys.
insights.implication: Plan two seasons of product: fieldhouse warmups for November to April and an outdoor drop in June. Refurbished fieldhouse floors do more good here than painted outdoor courts that spend months under snow.

insights.title: A Jordan city that grew up in Rose's adidas
insights.detail: Chicago is home to the 1985 Air Jordan 1 'Chicago' and still dresses its games in white, red and black, but a generation of South and West Side kids came up in adidas D Rose shoes and Rose's headband. Rose (adidas, plus the adidas-circuit Team Rose program), Candace Parker (adidas), Dwyane Wade (Li-Ning) and Angel Reese (Reebok, traded from the Sky to Atlanta in April 2026) mean many of the city's best-loved hoops names belong to rival brands.
insights.implication: Compete at the grassroots with Nike relationships: Mac Irvin Fire in the EYBL, the Bulls and Sky uniforms, and 'Chicago' color-blocking. Never borrow Rose's No. 1 or his Englewood story without him and his sponsor.

insights.title: 'Going downstate' and keeping kids home
insights.detail: IHSA official H.V. Porter is credited with coining 'March Madness' for the Illinois high school tournament in 1939, and 'going downstate' (Peoria or Champaign over the years) is still the goal of every season. College loyalty turns on whether Chicago's best stay in-state: the 1989 'Flyin' Illini' Final Four team leaned on Simeon's Nick Anderson, King's Marcus Liberty and Rich Central's Kendall Gill, and Morgan Park's Ayo Dosunmu chose Illinois in 2018, while Rose, Parker and Okafor left the state for college.
insights.implication: Treat March as a second peak: a state-tournament capsule built on bracket graphics, with a 'stay home, rep home' message. The words 'March Madness' themselves are a licensed mark.

insights.title: The calendar keeps going after the Bulls stop
insights.detail: The Sky won Chicago's first WNBA title in 2021 with Naperville's Candace Parker and play at Wintrust Arena in the South Loop alongside DePaul, and Angel Reese (traded to Atlanta in April 2026) and Kamilla Cardoso made Sky games a hot ticket from 2024. The G League's Windy City Bulls play in Hoffman Estates, and the NBA Draft Combine comes to Chicago every May.
insights.implication: Nike makes both NBA and WNBA uniforms, so a Bulls-Sky 'one city' line can keep Chicago hoops product selling from May to September. Lead with the team and the uniform; Reese no longer plays for the Sky.

insights.title: Chicago tells its hoops stories as documentaries
insights.detail: Kartemquin Films' 'Hoop Dreams' (1994, directed by Steve James) followed William Gates and Arthur Agee from the West Side through St. Joseph and Marshall, and Chicago filmmakers Coodie Simmons and Chike Ozah made ESPN's 30 for 30 'Benji' (2012). The Sun-Times' high school coverage still sets the daily Public League conversation.
insights.implication: The native activation format is long-form film. Commission a paid, credited series with Kartemquin or Coodie & Chike that follows a current Public League team through a season, with product tied to its episodes.
